clips.text_en_b1: I'm the biggest bull on /biz/, so take this seriously. The bond bear market is quickly becoming the worst in history. JGBs are moving in ways they haven't moved since 2003. Bond yields are breaking out, and gold is starting to lead. This can be read as bullish for hard assets.
clips.text_en_b2: I'm the biggest bull on /biz/, so take this seriously. While most people shrug off the warnings, the bond bear market is quickly turning into the worst in history. JGBs are moving in ways nobody has seen since 2003, and yields are breaking out across the board. Gold is starting to lead the charge, which can easily be read as a strong bullish signal for hard assets.
clips.text_en_c1: I consider myself the most committed bull on /biz/, and I would urge anyone reading to take what I'm about to say seriously. The bond bear market that we are presently enduring is rapidly cementing its place as the worst in recorded history, with JGBs exhibiting price action not witnessed since 2003. Yields are breaking out across the curve in a fashion that should alarm any serious participant, while gold has begun to lead hard assets higher, which by extension can reasonably be interpreted as a bullish signal. The macroeconomic implications, frankly, are rather severe.
clips.text_en_c2: Speaking as /biz/'s most committed bull, I urge you to read the underlying signal before dismissing it as hyperbole. What we are witnessing is, by any sober measure, the most punishing bond bear market in living memory, and the parallels with prior structural breaks are unsettling. Japanese Government Bonds are exhibiting volatility not seen since 2003, yields are decisively breaking out of multi-year consolidation, and gold has begun to lead the broader complex in a manner that cannot reasonably be dismissed as noise. Taken in concert, these movements constitute a tacit endorsement of hard assets, since they imply a coordinated repricing of credit risk. The implications for anyone still wedded to nominal yields are, I would gently suggest, profoundly uncomfortable.

clips.text_zh: 膠膠吶又有雞巴人話AI破解到math，所以所有coin都死。lol我BTC同ETH都揸緊，唔想睇但又唔走，擺明又被割🙏 個雞巴fe exam都未準備完又輸錢，我真係廢物。
clips.text_en_b1: OAI just one-shots 20% of outstanding math problems. Nerds on Xitter call for imminent breach of ECDSA cryptography, which means all coins break. This is clearly bullshit. But the fear alone is enough to ruin crypto. The market doesn't need the breakthrough to actually happen.
clips.text_en_b2: OAI just one-shots 20% of outstanding math problems overnight. Nerds on Xitter immediately jump to conclusions, calling for an imminent breach of ECDSA cryptography, which would supposedly break every coin in existence. This is clearly bullshit, but fear alone is enough to wreck crypto markets. The thing is, the market doesn't actually need the breakthrough to happen; panic does the damage.
clips.text_en_c1: OpenAI has reportedly demonstrated the capacity to one-shot roughly twenty percent of outstanding mathematical problems, a feat which, in the eyes of certain self-styled pundits on Xitter, constitutes an imminent threat to ECDSA cryptography. Should such a breakthrough materialise, the implications for cryptocurrency would be nothing short of catastrophic, with every coin in circulation effectively rendered worthless. The claim is, of course, arrant nonsense. Yet the market, being the irrational creature that it is, does not require the catastrophe to actually occur; the mere anticipation of it is sufficient to precipitate a rout.
clips.text_en_c2: Reports circulating that a frontier artificial intelligence system has, in a single inference pass, resolved some twenty per cent of the corpus's outstanding mathematical conjectures have, predictably, been weaponised by certain quarters of the crypto commentariat, who now solemnly proclaim the imminent collapse of ECDSA and, by extension, the entire edifice of public-key cryptography upon which every meaningful blockchain depends. The proposition is, plainly and without exaggeration, arrant nonsense. Yet the markets, being composed of human beings rather than Turing machines, do not require the catastrophe to materialise; the mere apprehension of it is sufficient to inflict damage. Fear, as any seasoned operator will attest, has never needed a corresponding fact to do its work.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread on AI math breakthrough panicking crypto holders

clips.text_zh: 又有4chan膠話Starlink會replace晒成個internet，跟住落CBDC同digital ID。即係Musk直接做咗全球嘅gatekeeper。🧐 我哋呢啲細香港人睇下就好，美國先係主場lol。
clips.text_en_b1: Elon Musk's Starlink will replace the old internet. This will be the chance to bring in CBDCs and digital ID. All online dissent will be wiped out. The next big false flag will be a 'cyber event' so they can justify shutting everything down. This was the plan before LLMs even existed.
clips.text_en_b2: Elon Musk's Starlink will inevitably replace the old internet we know. Once that happens, rolling out CBDCs and digital IDs becomes a breeze. All online dissent gets wiped out in one sweep, and the next big false flag will conveniently be some 'cyber event' so they can justify shutting everything down. Apparently this was the master plan long before LLMs even existed.
clips.text_en_c1: Elon Musk's Starlink constellation is poised, if certain commentators are to be believed, to supplant the legacy internet infrastructure upon which civilised discourse has hitherto depended. Should that substitution occur, the gateway would inevitably open for central bank digital currencies and, by extension, mandatory digital identification. All meaningful online dissent could, in such a scenario, be extinguished at the operator's discretion. The next manufactured pretext for a clampdown, it is widely speculated, will take the form of a so-called cyber event, ostensibly justifying the complete shutdown of dissent channels.
clips.text_en_c2: There is a strain of techno-libertarian reasoning on /g/ which contends that Elon Musk's Starlink constellation will, in relatively short order, render the legacy internet infrastructure obsolete, and that this consolidation will furnish the pretext for a wholesale migration toward central bank digital currencies and mandatory digital identity regimes. If one takes the thesis at face value, then a single private citizen effectively becomes the gatekeeper of global discourse, which should give even the most sanguine commentator pause. The corollary, advanced by those who have evidently been waiting for it, is that a manufactured cyber incident will provide the necessary casus belli for a comprehensive shutdown. Whether one finds this plausible depends largely on one's priors.
clips.source_hint: /g/ conspiracy thread about Starlink, CBDCs, digital ID

clips.text_zh: 打LOL打到悶，去4chan睇下V有咩講。有雞巴人話D&D game根本做唔到，因為你準備錯spell就要reload。lol我寧願打rank。晚上同肥仔信講下S15 lol。
clips.text_en_b1: How do you actually make a good D&D videogame? You go into a fight, you prepared the wrong spells, you die. You reload your save. You prepare spells for that specific fight you would never normally use. You win. That is not acceptable game design.
clips.text_en_b2: How do you actually make a good D&D videogame without ruining the experience? You walk into a fight, prepared the wrong spells, and die instantly. Then you reload your save, pick spells you would never normally use just for that specific encounter, and breeze through it. That cycle is fundamentally broken game design, since it removes any meaningful consequence from your choices.
clips.text_en_c1: A question that has long vexed the /v/ board concerns how one might conceivably translate the Dungeons and Dragons experience into a workable video game format. The fundamental issue, as any seasoned player will readily attest, is that combat invariably rewards preparation tailored to a specific encounter. Should you fail to memorise the precise spell required for a given adversary, death follows almost immediately, prompting a reload of an earlier save. You then select precisely those spells you would never have chosen organically, and victory, such as it is, is yours. That is not acceptable game design.
clips.text_en_c2: The question of how one might actually construct a defensible Dungeons & Dragons adaptation for interactive media has long vexed the /v/ faithful, and the canonical objection bears repeating. A player enters a hostile encounter, has neglected to memorise the appropriate spells for that particular opposition, suffers an inglorious defeat, returns to a prior save state, and retroactively selects the optimal loadout. The encounter is then trivialised. This is not, in any meaningful sense, design; it is merely arithmetic with a graphical veneer. The experience erodes, by degrees, the entire premise of a tabletop-inspired system, namely that preparation is consequential. Without that, one might as well be playing a spreadsheet.
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread complaining about save-scumming in D&D RPGs

clips.text_zh: 睇到4chan /fit/ 有條post問同gf一齊gym。lol我單身30年，淨係同肥仔信一齊做。屌，做完gym返到屋企得一個人，好撚靜。算啦，拎鐵係真。
clips.text_en_b1: Do you lift with your woman, /fit/? My sister was into fitness way before me, so my girlfriend has a gym buddy she can do her girly routine with, while I go lift real weights. Couples who train together usually end up with one doing the actual work.
clips.text_en_b2: Do you lift with your woman, /fit/? My sister was into fitness way before I ever touched a barbell, so my girlfriend already has a gym buddy for her girly routine, while I get on with the serious work. Honestly, couples who train together usually end up with one partner doing all the actual lifting while the other phones it in.
clips.text_en_c1: A thread on /fit/ recently invited a decent view of whether one ought, as a matter of routine, to train alongside one's romantic partner. My sister, who happens to have been deeply into fitness long before I ever picked up a barbell, serves as the ideal gym companion for my girlfriend; she can perform all manner of unremarkable girly routines to her heart's content, while I proceed to lift what might charitably be described as actual weight. Couples who train together invariably discover that one party ends up shouldering the disproportionate share of the work.
clips.text_en_c2: A perennial thread on /fit/ revisits the question of whether couples ought to train together, and the consensus, such as it is, tends toward the unromantic. The poster's sister, by his own admission, was a committed enthusiast long before he discovered the iron, and his partner has wisely arranged her programming around a female training companion with whom she can pursue her lighter, more aesthetically-oriented work, leaving him free to pursue the serious business of progressive overload. The pattern he identifies is depressingly universal: one party performs the actual labour, while the other essentially supervises. There is, I suspect, a metaphor here for relationships more broadly, but I shall leave that exercise to the reader.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread on lifting with your girlfriend vs alone

clips.text_zh: 4chan /a/ 有人話晒啲shonen都係重覆又重覆嘅hero journey。AOT我都睇晒，講真結局係頂癮。我宜家睇緊Demon Slayer，幾勁但真係長過我份GI report。🧐
clips.text_en_b1: Hot take: most shonen anime are a flawed hero's journey forced on loop. Most shonen would be better if they ended at season one. Stuff like Attack on Titan, Naruto, and One Piece just spam mini hero journeys for hundreds of episodes. I'd rather read a whole story in 3 hours.
clips.text_en_b2: Hot take from /a/: most shonen anime are essentially a flawed hero's journey forced on repeat. If most series had the guts to wrap up at season one, the genre would be far stronger for it. Instead, franchises like Attack on Titan, Naruto, and One Piece spam mini hero journeys for hundreds of episodes, padding out filler until the story loses all momentum.
clips.text_en_c1: A rather contentious proposition has resurfaced on /a/ of late, namely that the overwhelming majority of shonen anime are fundamentally the same flawed hero's journey, reheated and re-served ad infinitum. Were these series to conclude at the end of their inaugural season, the consensus appears to be that the source material would be materially improved. Titles such as Attack on Titan, Naruto, and One Piece, it is argued, simply regurgitate variations of the same monomyth for hundreds upon hundreds of episodes. One might reasonably prefer to consume a complete narrative within the space of a single afternoon.
clips.text_en_c2: A somewhat unfashionable opinion circulating on /a/ holds that the majority of long-running shonen series are, at their structural core, the same flawed hero's journey played on an apparently infinite loop, with diminishing returns that the format itself seems constitutionally incapable of acknowledging. Were the industry to exhibit even a modicum of editorial discipline, the argument runs, most of these properties would benefit immeasurably from concluding at the close of their first proper arc. Consider how Detention, Naruto, and the like have, over hundreds of episodes, iterated upon a fundamentally identical template until the viewer's patience is exhausted. A three-hour commitment, yielding a complete narrative arc, increasingly looks like a better bargain than anything currently on offer.
